articles.title: Future of Marketing Briefing: Creators had a big year. Christmas still went to the celebrities
articles.summary: Despite leaning on creators for most of the year, marketers aren’t doing it for the holiday crunch. That job still belongs to celebrities.
articles.excerpt: Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit Creators are everywhere in marketing these days — everywhere except Christmas ads. The first batch of festive campaigns, from John Lewis, SharkNinja, Ulta Beauty and Burberry among others, makes little for the industry’s favorite obsession. Despite leaning on creators throughout the rest of the year, marketers aren’t doing it for the holiday crunch. That job still belongs to celebrities. Sephora has cast Seth Rogen as a man hopelessly out of his depth, rescued by one of the retailer’s Beauty Advisors before he can do any lasting damage. Over at Kay, Saturday Night Live’s Colin Jost is put through that most well-worn of Christmas tropes: the frantic hunt for the perfect present for someone special. Sports Direct roped in Nike to push the cliche a step further. Its ad follows an uncle wandering the aisles in search of something for his niece, blissfully unaware that a squad of Nike athletes is quietly steering him to the right choice. And Gucci has Mariah Carey — the industry version of the relative who gets passed from house to house every December. This year it’s the luxury brand’s turn to host her. Why these brands do this year after year is no secret. Celebrities, particularly the calibre fronting this year’s crop, are the advertising equivalent of tinsel: nobody calls it innovative but a tree looks bare without it. For CMOs wary of how quickly an ad can set off the internet these days, that familiarity is a safety blanket. John Lewis is the latest case. Within a day of release, its spot had Piers Morgan calling it “possibly the worst advert I’ve ever seen for anything” and Mumsnet testing into the “ungrateful” grandchildren. Dame Kristin Scott Thomas, the ad’s star, escaped without a scratch.

articles.excerpt: Alphabet’s Q3 numbers show AI Mode growing faster than it earns, and every reason Google gave for the slowdown is temporary except one. Alphabet just reported the fastest growth in Google search queries in five years; in the same quarter, its search revenue grew at the slowest rate in 2026. Roger covered the earnings call earlier this week on Search Engine Journal , and it’s a great overview of the high points. I’m diving deeper to make a specific point here. Search & other revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion in the third quarter, according to Alphabet’s earnings release , down from 19% in the first quarter and 17% in the second . That was roughly $1.6 billion below analyst expectations, and CNBC reported it was the second straight quarter search came in under estimates. On the earnings call , Google’s chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, named one of the causes directly: strong growth in AI Mode queries “had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.” For two years, the argument over whether AI answers cut into search has run on inferred numbers: click-through studies , panel estimates, and referral samples, many from vendors with something to sell. This quarter, the effect shows up in a counted number, Google’s own revenue line, with a Google executive naming AI Mode as a cause. That changes the quality of the evidence, even if it doesn’t finalize the argument. A quick disclosure before going further: I run a company that measures visibility inside AI answers, so a story about money moving into those answers isn’t neutral ground for me. The market reaction was severe. Alphabet shares fell about 13% on Thursday, the steepest one-day drop on record, erasing roughly half a trillion dollars in market value . Students, educators and IT teams are putting AI to work in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects that build pathways into industry. Alongside this work, universities are developing frameworks for where and how AI can be used in learning and assessment, helping students build practical skills while knowing when to rely on their own judgment. For teachers, employers and industry practitioners, these examples offer practical lessons in designing AI-supported learning, setting clear expectations for AI use and preparing Australians for an AI-enabled workplace. articles.excerpt: Retailers investing in AI ahead of Peak 2026 risk focusing on operational efficiencies while overlooking the delivery fundamentals that matter most to shoppers, according to new research from Scurri . Two studies of UK retailers and consumers show businesses accelerating their use of AI to tackle rising costs and increasingly complex customer journeys. But shoppers want to keep delivery affordable, be told when their order will arrive and get communications quickly when something goes wrong. 64% of consumers worry retailers are using AI mainly to reduce costs. Among retailers, business efficiency is one of the leading reasons for AI adoption, cited by 32%. Yet shoppers appear less interested in the technology than the outcome. When waiting for an order, 53% say real-time tracking matters most and 44% prioritise an accurate delivery date. Almost half (47%) would accept a Peak order arriving late if they had been warned in advance. The findings also challenge the assumption that Peak shoppers demand even faster fulfilment. Free delivery matters to 61%, compared with 29% prioritising next day delivery and just 13% same day. Two thirds (67%) would accept longer delivery times during Peak in return for free or cheaper delivery. The Peak battleground may therefore be shifting from speed towards certainty and value. Retailers are looking to AI to help deliver this. Almost six in ten (58%) say they are likely to use automated AI to manage ecommerce delivery strategy and carrier operations, while retailers estimate AI automation of carrier management could reduce delivery costs by an average of 10.6%. articles.summary: 73% of ‘Premium Gamers’ view new games releases as overpriced at launch and actively wait until prices drop, according to new research. The post Premium Gamers’ discount-first mentality reflects wider retail shift towards value appeared first on InternetRetailing .
articles.excerpt: 73% of ‘Premium Gamers’ view new games releases as overpriced at launch and actively wait until prices drop, according to new research into the gaming industry. G2A and Newzoo’s global study ‘ Game purchasing behavior in an era of choice ’ looked at the buying and playing patterns of 6,000 respondents across the UK, US, Germany, Poland, Saudi Arabia, and Brazil, and found that price sensitivity is a key behavioural driver. On average, ‘Premium Gamers’ – defined as monthly PC or Gen 9 console users who accessed AAA or AA games in the past year, either by purchasing them or through a premium subscription – wait until a game’s price is discounted by 29% to 45% before purchase. They expect worthwhile discounts around five months after launch. Premium Gamers are most likely to be console users, male, and under 35, according to the study. Despite having a huge range of choice, many relatively old titles still dominate the mix of games played by Premium Gamers, and despite being buyers, 38% of the titles they played over the last year were free to play. Most games are purchased from official storefronts, with only Amazon and Loaded (the reseller formerly known as CDKeys) appearing in the top 10 list of how Premium Gamers buy games. 19% were paid for by a subscription, with most Premium Gamers agreeing that subscriptions enable game discovery, offer good discounts and promotions, and support or enhance the multiplayer experience. The results of the study come ahead of the launch of Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI, scheduled for 19 November – one of the most hotly-anticipated releases of the decade, coming a whopping 13 years after GTA V. articles.excerpt: In the web’s early days, developers placed a summary of links to a site’s key sections, such as categories, company pages, policies, and more. The summaries could appear in footers or on standalone pages. Developers called the summaries “sitemaps.” In 2005, Google introduced a new version of sitemaps based on Extensible Markup Language, a 1990s text-based format for storing data, that site owners could submit to Google (via what became Search Console). The aim was to help search engines crawl and index all pages on a site. In time, the industry referred to the versions as “HTML sitemaps” and “XML sitemaps.” XML sitemaps help with discoverability. Search engines can find pages quickly in the sitemap without landing on the site itself. Whether the search-engine bots access and index the newly discovered pages depends on crawl budget, site authority, content relevance, depth and originality , internal linking, and external backlinks, among other signals. Conversely, HTML sitemaps provide no backdoor to a site. Crawlers must land on a site to access an HTML sitemap, likely via internal links. Search engine optimizers disagree on the impact of HTML sitemaps. In my experience, such sitemaps likely help indexing by revealing the internal links to every page. When placed in the footer, HTML sitemaps spread internal link equity to the listed pages. They minimize the number of pages in Search Console’s “ Crawled, currently not indexed ” status. Both sitemaps — HTML and XML — help search engines discover, crawl, and index more pages, especially on larger sites. But neither replaces a website hierarchy that naturally prioritizes important pages. Only a fast, well-structured, and well-interlinked website ensures solid organic search visibility. To avoid further fines, Temu submitted an action plan in August, which has now been approved by the European Commission. The platform has committed to implementing five corrective measures. These are intended to help Temu better identify and address the risks associated with illegal products on its platform. Temu must conduct a platform-specific risk assessment, measure the effectiveness of its measures against illegal products, and investigate shortcomings in its product controls and content moderation systems. In addition, the company must examine how its recommendation algorithms could amplify the spread of illegal products and investigate how sellers might manipulate the platform to offer such items. Temu has four months to implement the measures, after which an independent audit will assess their implementation. It wasn’t so long ago that Boxing Day was the undisputed king of the British sales calendar. Shoppers queued outside department stores in the early hours, scrapped over discounted white goods, and descended on the high street to panic buy piles of cut-price clothes and Christmas stock. Next thing you know, Black Friday arrives from America and the party is over. These days, Black Friday is an obsession for retail marketers, with huge budgets, months of planning and increasingly elaborate campaigns geared towards getting customers to part with their cash. And while there’s no questioning its importance, it’s worth considering whether all this attention is coming at the expense of other opportunities throughout the Christmas and holiday sales season. After all, there’s little point fighting tooth and nail for Black Friday customers if good sales opportunities are being missed later in the quarter. Because Boxing Day, despite playing second fiddle in the public’s cultural consciousness, still has plenty to offer. Adobe reports that UK consumers spent £1.16 billion online during Black Friday 2025, making it the biggest online shopping day of the year. It’s an enormous opportunity, and understandably one that retailers are keen to capitalise on. The danger comes when brands put too much faith in a single event. articles.excerpt: A family-owned florist in Spain tracked ChatGPT-driven orders and found revenue blooming. “Your 22 October column, ‘ AI Shopping Metrics Considered ‘, and ‘ Mixed Reports on AI Ecommerce Traffic ‘ from April are why I’m writing,” explained José Pérez Sánchez of Persa Flores in an email message. “Since September 2026, one in five of our online orders has come from someone who found us in ChatGPT.” Pérez Sánchez had used his company’s own data to extend the arguments made in those earlier articles. He says AI-referred shoppers are difficult to identify without order-level attribution. Persa Flores, a Spain-based florist, has received 20% of online orders from ChatGPT since September. “For every order, Shopify records the customer’s first and last visit before buying: where they came from, the referring site, the landing page with its full URL, and the date,” wrote Pérez Sánchez in response to questions about how his business identified which sources lead to sales. “We count an order as ChatGPT when either [the first or last] visit came from ChatGPT or OpenAI,” Pérez Sánchez explained. “Every one of these orders arrived on a link tagged utm_source=chatgpt.com , which ChatGPT adds itself. [But] only about one in eight also showed ChatGPT as the referrer, so a shop that checks referrers alone will miss most of this traffic.” The missing data can be confusing, and so can the word. In technical parlance, the word “referrer” is traditionally misspelled as “referer.” Regardless, a “referrer” is a visitor’s last URL before arriving at the target website. A web browser passes the referrer in the HTTP header, where various analytics tools read it.
